entries.title: Means of Transport (relative costs of sea, river and road)
entries.summary: Compares the cost and speed of sea, river and road travel, which the rest of the chapter uses for planning journeys and cargo.
quotes: River travel is about twice as expensive as sea travel

entries.title: Vessels and Cargo Capacity
entries.summary: Defines the tun as the unit of cargo capacity used for all vessels, land and water.
quotes: a ton of cargo takes up as much space and carrying capacity as a tun

entries.title: Land Vessels (pack animals and carts)
entries.summary: Load capacities, costs, road requirements and crew needs for pack animals and carts.
quotes: A single person can effectively lead and tend three pack beasts if walking with a halter to the first beast, or six if riding.

entries.title: River Barges
entries.summary: Capacity and crew of river barges and lighters, which vary with the depth of the water.
quotes: Optimally, they have three crewmembers, but many have only a man and a boy.

entries.title: Seagoing Ships (buss, cog, galley, nef)
entries.summary: Describes the main seagoing ship types with typical cargo capacity, crew and cost, including limits on ship size and the larger crews of southern lateen-rigged ships.
quotes: A sailing ship costs four pounds per ten tons of cargo it can carry.

entries.title: Comparison of Traveling Speeds
entries.summary: Gives ranges of miles per day for river barges, road cargoes, riders, coaches, couriers and sailing ships, in standard miles.
quotes: Sailing vessels travel roughly 60 to 80 miles per day.
River barges travel 8 to 10 miles per day, faster downriver than upriver.

entries.title: Comparison of Traveling Costs
entries.summary: Passage prices and relative costs for sea, river and road travel, chartering a ship, the surcharge for known magi, and the profit a carrier typically keeps.
quotes: River travel costs twice as much as sea travel.
Known magi may need to offer double their usual fee for passage

entries.title: Adding Places to the Land Trade Map and Naval Trade Tables
entries.summary: A procedure for working out travel times to new places by dividing direct distance by a set figure for road, river with or against the current, or sea, plus a note on standard versus nautical miles.
quotes: Divide that distance by 12 for road travel.
For sea travel, divide the direct distance by 60.

entries.title: Naval Trade Tables
entries.summary: Sidebar tables of sea travel times between ports in six regions, joined by junctions; a voyage is planned by adding the times to each junction and then to the final port.
quotes: A player designing a voyage simply adds together the times to each junction, then to the final port.

entries.title: Troupe-Style Roleplaying
entries.summary: Explains why troupe-style play, in which players have several characters and the storyguide role can be shared, suits Ars Magica better than conventional single-character play given how different magi, companions and grogs are.
quotes: it is almost always better to use some version of troupe-style play rather than conventional play

entries.title: Alternative Characters (Troupe Style)
entries.summary: Each player has two or more characters, at least one a magus and one a companion, but plays only one per session, so the characters need good reasons not to adventure together.
quotes: In this version of troupe-style play each player has two or more characters, but only plays one of them in a given session.

entries.title: Pooled Characters (Troupe Style)
entries.summary: A shared pool of grogs and bit-part characters that any player can run, each looked after between sessions by a single player; keeps magi few, lets grogs die safely, and handles player absences because advancement does not depend on being played.
quotes: in addition to a player's magi and companions, there is also a 'pool' of grogs and bit-parts, who can be played by anyone.

entries.title: Guest Storyguiding
entries.summary: A player occasionally runs a session while the regular storyguide plays pooled grogs; best used for isolated stories such as a distant island or a regio, agreeing in advance on rewards and risks.
quotes: The next level of troupe-style playing involves a player occasionally running a session.

entries.title: Alpha and Beta Storyguides
entries.summary: Several people storyguide regularly: an alpha storyguide with veto power over the saga's overall shape and beta storyguides each responsible for a location or aspect, who must agree on reward level and tone.
quotes: One storyguide, the alpha storyguide, is responsible for the overall shape of the saga, and has final veto power on story additions

entries.title: Pure Troupe Style
entries.summary: Everyone storyguides in roughly equal amounts with no alpha storyguide, requiring an agreed method, such as a rules storyguide, for resolving rules disputes.
quotes: In the purest form of troupe style, everyone runs games in roughly equal amounts, and there is no alpha storyguide.

entries.title: Saga Background: History
entries.summary: The troupe decides how closely the saga follows real history, how much mundane interaction there is, and whether magi can change history after the canonical start date.
quotes: The troupe must simply decide whether the magi can change history.

entries.title: Saga Background: The Church
entries.summary: Choices for portraying the Church in a saga: basically good or basically evil, and whether it treats magic as sinful or as a God-given gift.
quotes: The fundamental choice is between a Church which is basically good with a few bad members, is basically evil, with a few good members.

entries.title: Researching a Setting
entries.summary: Describes levels of historical research a storyguide can put into a saga, from a pure fantasy world and no-research through low, medium, high and extreme research, with practical steps for each.
quotes: There are a number of options for this, and none is better or worse than the others.

entries.title: Saga Styles
entries.summary: Seven compatible styles of saga to choose or combine: high fantasy, mundane interactions, Hermetic life, action-adventure, investigation, politics and creation.
quotes: all valid, and many compatible with each other

entries.title: Saga Priorities
entries.summary: Puts player enjoyment first: talk through content that upsets players, let players adapt characters to the stories they like, and treat game balance only as a tool for sharing the spotlight when changing rules.
quotes: The highest priority for any saga is to ensure that all the players are having fun.
As long as the changes help everyone to have fun, they are good.

entries.title: Saga Speed
entries.summary: Introduces saga speed, the number of game seasons that pass per session, as a key choice that sets the style of a saga and can be changed later.
quotes: the number of seasons of game time that pass for every game session is an extremely important factor in determining the style of a saga

entries.title: Slow Saga
entries.summary: A saga with two or more sessions per season: characters barely improve and lifespans hardly matter, laboratory rules see little use, and Virtues and Flaws affecting starting scores matter more than those affecting study or lifespan.
quotes: In a slow saga there are, on average, two or more game sessions per season.

entries.title: Medium Saga
entries.summary: A saga with one to four seasons per session: a good compromise and starting rate in which characters improve, companions and grogs may eventually die of old age, and study-related Flaws weigh about as much as starting-score ones.
quotes: A medium saga has, on average, one to four seasons per game session.

entries.title: Fast Saga
entries.summary: A saga where more than a year passes per session: magi grow powerful quickly and may die of old age within it, companions are played only a few times, and Virtues and Flaws affecting only starting scores lose importance.
quotes: In a fast saga, more than one year passes per game session, on average.

entries.title: Pulsed Saga
entries.summary: A saga alternating bursts of intense play over a short span with long gaps of years, giving companions and grogs play time while magi advance during the downtime, at the cost of needing an in-game reason for the quiet periods.
quotes: A dozen game sessions might cover a single season, but then twelve game years might pass before the next session.

entries.title: Running an Establishment
entries.summary: General system for the quality, capacity, upkeep and staffing of kennels, mews and stables, including what happens when maintenance is not paid; includes a modifiable gyrfalcon template for other hawks and falcons.
quotes: Reduce the number of animals by 15% (round up) for each season these requirements are not met.
Failure to meet the annual maintenance cost results in the establishment dropping to the next lower level of quality immediately.

entries.title: The Kennels
entries.summary: What a kennel contains, giving the standard mix of hound types and how larger qualities scale it up.
quotes: for every 12 running dogs there is one lymer and three greyhounds or alaunts

entries.title: Kennels, Mews, and Stables Tables
entries.summary: Tables giving capacity, yearly maintenance cost, staff and Living Conditions modifier for each quality of kennel, mews and stables.

entries.title: Living Conditions and Specialists
entries.summary: The specialist Ability needed to benefit from an establishment's positive Living Conditions modifier, and the yearly winter roll that decides whether it is well run or declines.
quotes: A stress roll of Intelligence + Animal Handling against Ease Factor 9
a score in the relevant Profession Ability equal to at least twice the Living Conditions modifier

entries.title: The Manor: The Model Fief
entries.summary: Defines the manor as the basic game unit of fief, the land needed to support a knight and household, and lists what a typical manor contains.
quotes: A manor, for the purposes of the game, comprises the amount of land traditionally required to maintain a knight, his family, and his household retainers.

related.text: LoM Chapter Three: A Comparison of Titles

entries.title: How Big is a…?
entries.summary: Reference sizes and incomes for acres, manors, hides, virgates, bovates, cottars, villages, towns and cities, with the typical split of peasant holdings and a Terram magic scale for an acre of earth.
quotes: For the sake of simplicity an acre is considered to be 4,840 square yards.
A landed knight's income from a typical manor is twenty pounds per year
Twenty percent have a full virgate, thirty percent have a bovate, and fifty percent are cottars.

entries.title: Farmland
entries.summary: The six legal statuses a piece of land can have and the main land types on a heavily farmed manor.
quotes: Each piece of land has one of six legal statuses.

entries.title: How Small is the Ruling Class of a Kingdom?
entries.summary: Counts of baronies, greater barons and knight's fees in England, showing how small and interrelated the ruling class is, with a note on squires who avoid knighthood for tax reasons.
quotes: These 45 men are all closely related to each other by blood and marriage.

entries.title: The German System
entries.summary: Explains the three sources of German titles (imperial, allodial and local) and their relative status, used to compare German ranks with the French system.
quotes: Assume that an imperial knight has higher status than a free knight, who has higher status than a common knight.

entries.title: Iberian Systems
entries.summary: How Iberian town charters (fueros) shape military service, with a simplified model in which every householder serves unless exempted, fighting either on foot as peons or on horse as caballeros.
quotes: As a simplified version of this model, all people who own a house are expected to serve, unless they have an exemption due to a clause in the fuero.

entries.title: Church Calendar (holy days and the Dominion)
entries.summary: Sidebar listing Christian holy days and seasons, noting the Dominion dips on the eve of major holidays and that Faerie and Magical powers may ignore Dominion penalties during the Christmas season.
quotes: The Dominion tends to lower significantly on the eve preceding a major holiday
storyguides may wish to allow appropriate Faerie and Magical powers to ignore penalties from the Dominion during these days

entries.title: Excommunication
entries.summary: Describes excommunication and its game effects: loss of sacramental benefits, treatment as unbaptized, loss of Confidence or Faith Point increases, and restoration through the sacrament of penance.
quotes: Any increase of Confidence or Faith Points the character has received are immediately lost.

entries.title: The Champagne Cycle (fair calendar and trading order)
entries.summary: Sidebar giving the dates and durations of the Champagne fairs and how trade in each six-week fair is regulated into set-up, cloth, leather, other goods and settling of accounts.
quotes: Generally there is an interval of about two weeks in between fairs.

entries.title: The English Fair Cycle (fair calendar and owners)
entries.summary: Sidebar listing the major English fairs with their dates and owners.
quotes: Stamford: Ash Wednesday to Palm Sunday (owner: Earl Warenne)

entries.title: Horses
entries.summary: Explains that medieval horses are classed by role rather than breed, the status and cost issues of owning horses, and the roles of mares and stallions in farming, travel and war.
quotes: Medieval horses are not differentiated from one another by breed, but rather by their suitability for certain roles.

entries.title: A Note on Size and Capacity
entries.summary: Explains how horses are measured in hands and gives a rule of thumb for how much weight a horse can carry unencumbered.
quotes: A horse can carry unencumbered about 30% of its weight in pounds

entries.title: Becoming a Monk or Nun
entries.summary: The procedure for entering a religious house: harsh testing on arrival, a probationary year as a novice, the three solemn vows, and rules on oblates and the admission of girls to nunneries.
quotes: The three chief vows that are sworn as solemn oaths are for chastity, poverty, and obedience.

entries.title: The Opus Dei, Divine Office
entries.summary: A timetable of the canonical hours, meals and chapter meetings in a monastery, giving the storyguide a guide to where monks are and what they are doing at any hour.
quotes: Roused from sleep by the sacristan with a bell, the monks attend the first service of the day.

entries.title: Mythic Options: The Nobility
entries.summary: Optional ways to put more magic into the nobility, such as faerie lords, supernatural noble lines, magical rulers or enchanted items of succession, to be used as much or as little as the troupe wants.
quotes: If you want to keep medieval society fairly mundane, you shouldn't use any of them.

entries.title: Mythic Options: Towns and Trade
entries.summary: Optional ways to make towns more magical, such as faerie towns, supernatural traders, or a town that is a living being aligned to a realm.
quotes: A town might be alive as a whole, and aligned to any realm.

entries.title: Variable Outcomes
entries.summary: Storyguide guidance to give every story at least success, neutral and failure outcomes, to avoid disastrous consequences for failure, and to prefer setbacks like lost possessions or lost study time over character or covenant destruction.
quotes: You should have at least three possible outcomes for any story: one corresponding to success, another to a neutral performance, and one to failure.

entries.title: Story Types (Reactive, Proactive, Soap Opera)
entries.summary: Divides stories into reactive, proactive and soap opera types and explains how each works as the magi grow more powerful, since powerful magi short-circuit reactive and investigative plots.
quotes: this discussion divides stories into three types: reactive, where something happens and the player characters respond

entries.title: Student-Run University
entries.summary: Describes the southern, student-governed model of university and gives sample statutes that bind masters, such as lecture attendance, original instruction and hosting disputationes.
quotes: A master must host a disputatio at least once a term.
A master may not read directly from the text during his lecture, but must offer commentaries and arguments that gloss the text.

entries.title: University of Masters
entries.summary: Describes the northern, master-governed model of university and gives sample statutes that bind students, such as dress, curfew, language and matriculation.
quotes: A student must always speak Latin, at class and in his residence.
A student must be matriculated into his faculty and must swear his Oath of Matriculation.

entries.title: Hawking
entries.summary: How noble hawking works: the hawker rolls to release and command the bird, and a results table says how aggressively the hawk attacks its prey.
quotes: The mechanics of hunting require a Presence + Animal Handling roll from the hawker, as he releases the hawk and issues commands.

entries.title: Rules Questions (House Rules)
entries.summary: Advice on when the Laboratory and Long-Term Event rules matter and on adopting house rules, with examples such as using only simple dice, adding trade rules, giving mundane believers a Magic Resistance, or dropping statistics altogether.
quotes: you can simply ignore stress dice, and always use a simple die
You might decide to give all Christians, Jews, and Muslims a Magic Resistance equal to five times the level of the local Dominion aura.

entries.title: How Much Do Nobles Know?
entries.summary: What nobles typically know, believe and misunderstand about the Order of Hermes, from the facts almost all of them know to the extra knowledge of scholarly senior nobles and the misconceptions spread by House Jerbiton. Sidebars cover how nobles lodge pleas, harm to cities and special Magic Resistance for rulers and Church officers.
quotes: Educated nobles may have low Order of Hermes Lore scores, and those who have family members — either current or ancestral — associated with House Jerbiton may know far more.

entries.title: Why Don't Magi Break Mythic European Feudalism?
entries.summary: Offers several optional ways a troupe can explain, or ignore, why magi leave feudal society largely unchanged: ignoring it, a Code that simply works, coincidence, or hidden realm forces such as God's plan, demonic temptation, faeries or magi who designed feudalism.
quotes: Troupes should discuss their approach to the impact of magi on society when designing their sagas, selecting an approach that suits the stories they wish to tell.
Ignoring the elements of the setting that don't seamlessly cohere between Mythic and historical Europe is the simplest solution, and the one suggested for most troupes.

entries.title: Un-Fun History (Adjusting the Setting)
entries.summary: Guidance for troupes who dislike parts of medieval society: they may gloss over or remove unpalatable features, play the oppressed, or lean on the Order of Hermes as a tolerant home base.
quotes: The Order of Hermes is deliberately designed to be anachronistic and fundamentally tolerant

entries.title: Discuss Poverty in Your Saga
entries.summary: Optional guidance for the troupe on how realistic the saga's treatment of peasant hardship, noble villainy and Church oppression should be, including simply choosing a covenant's peasants to be happy at creation.
quotes: Troupes should discuss this and choose a degree of realism that suits the stories they wish to tell.

entries.title: Becoming a Townsman (Citizenship and Sympathetic Connection)
entries.summary: Explains what it takes for a character to become a burgess of a chartered town, and that citizenship creates a sympathetic connection with everyone living under the same charter that can be used to aid magical attacks.
quotes: provide a +1 multiplier bonus to the Penetration score of a magical attack
live in the town continuously for a year and a day

entries.title: Town Occupations Table
entries.summary: A table giving the share of a town's population working in agriculture, craft, service and trade by town size.

entries.title: Commercial Sources of Trade Goods (reading the lists)
entries.summary: Explains how to read the regional lists of trade goods: only major export sources are listed, italics mark famous exporters, and cheap or fine markers say which qualities are available.
quotes: If a commodity is marked as cheap, then only standard and shoddy goods are available at that rate, while commodities marked fine include superior and excellent versions.

entries.title: Novelties (optional technologies for trade)
entries.summary: Optional innovations (business correspondence, deposit banking, insurance, letters of exchange, rudders, saws, vertical integration and others) that magi could introduce to change trade in a saga.
quotes: Most cranes can handle only about two and a half tons of carefully stowed cargo

entries.title: Trade
entries.summary: How this book treats non-agricultural income: as part of agricultural income or a simple bonus to it, with characters who trade seriously using the City & Guild rules.
quotes: non-agricultural sources of wealth are treated either as an unremarked component of agricultural income or as a bonus to the character's agricultural income.

entries.title: Weights and Measures (unit conversions)
entries.summary: Sidebar of conversion tables for length, capacity, weight, and the separate scales used for gold and silver and for apothecaries, as a guide to retail units.
quotes: 4 quarts = 1 gallon
16 ounces = 1 pound

entries.title: Women as Warriors
entries.summary: Notes how cultures react to women acting as knights and the Hermetic attitude toward it, with five historical examples (dressing as a man, inheritance, conquest, absence and political success) to guide backgrounds for female nobles seeking military roles.
quotes: The following examples may guide the generation of background for female nobles who seek military roles.

entries.title: Bath: Rumors (what is known by category)
entries.summary: Bath's application of the lore-roll system: the roll uses Area Lore (or Organization Lore: Church with penalties by distance), and sorted lists show what is known at each of the four knowledge levels.
quotes: Players can make an Intelligence + Area Lore: Stonehenge Tribunal to see what their characters know.

related.text: Mythic Locations: What the Magi Know

entries.title: Bear Island: What the Magi Know (lore rolls)
entries.summary: Bear Island's specific lore rolls: Area Lore (Anatolia or Theban Tribunal) with a bonus for eastern magi, or Artes Liberales with a penalty, followed by what is known at each knowledge level.
quotes: The legend is more popular in the east than the west, and an eastern magus receives a +3 bonus.
This roll is penalized by –6, because the Legend of the Golden Fleece is not popular or readily accessible.

related.text: Mythic Locations: What the Magi Know

entries.title: Cursewood: What is Known of Regulus (lore roll)
entries.summary: An Intelligence + Organization Lore: Order of Hermes roll to learn about Regulus, modified by training at his covenant or outside the Rhine Tribunal, with lists of what is known at each knowledge level.
quotes: players roll Intelligence + Organization Lore: Order of Hermes
Magi trained outside the Rhine Tribunal suffer a -3 modifier to the roll.

related.text: Mythic Locations: What the Magi Know

entries.title: Cursewood: What is Known about Pomerania (lore roll)
entries.summary: An Intelligence + Area Lore: Pomerania roll at the first mention of the Cursewood, with the knowledge levels it unlocks.
quotes: At the first mention of the Cursewood, players may make a roll of Intelligence + Area Lore: Pomerania.

related.text: Mythic Locations: What the Magi Know

entries.title: Farne Islands: What You've Heard (lore rolls)
entries.summary: Locals get a bonus to Area Lore rolls about the islands, followed by what is known at each knowledge level.
quotes: Locals get a +3 bonus to their Area Lore: Northumberland rolls for what they know about the Farne Islands.

related.text: Mythic Locations: What the Magi Know

entries.title: Arable
entries.summary: How cropland is used and the average sowing rates and yields of winter and spring grain.
quotes: The average winter grain crop is sown at two bushels an acre, and repays that effort with eight bushels of grain.

entries.title: Pasture
entries.summary: Typical flock sizes, grazing rents and shares of sheep, pigs, goats and cattle on a manor.
quotes: As a general rule, the lord has two-thirds of the sheep of any manor in his demesne flock.

entries.title: Two or Three Field Rotation
entries.summary: How crops are rotated through fields under the two-field and three-field systems, and how the manor court decides what is planted in each furlong.
quotes: In a three-field manor, wheat or rye is planted in autumn in the first field.

entries.title: June
entries.summary: June duties including shearing and plowing, Midsummer beliefs, and how quickly a laborer can cut hay, with the fire risk from damp stacked hay.
quotes: Each laborer can cut about an acre a day in good weather.

entries.title: Improvement
entries.summary: When non-magical lords invest in improving their lands, depending on how secure their holdings are.

entries.title: Assarting
entries.summary: Clearing fertile waste into cropland or meadow, how fast a laborer can do it, and how magic can assart land and alarm neighboring lords.
quotes: A single strong laborer with proper tools clears one acre of lightly wooded land per month, if he does no other work.

entries.title: Land Management
entries.summary: Assumes manors have a competent bailiff, so characters cannot improve land just by managing it better unless it was noted as badly run, and says customary businesses are already counted in manor income.
quotes: It is assumed in this section that characters cannot improve their lands simply by managing them better

entries.title: Purchase
entries.summary: Buying land from neighbors costs a multiple of its annual income, adjustable if the seller keeps rights or the buyer takes on dues, and cheaper if paid in immediate coin.
quotes: Characters may purchase land from their neighbors.
Characters can get a better price by paying in immediate coin

entries.title: Templar Papal Privileges
entries.summary: List of the legal and religious privileges granted to the Templars by papal bulls, such as keeping booty, freedom from tithes and oaths to outsiders, and their own clergy; useful for adjudicating how Templars interact with Church and lay authority.
quotes: The order may keep the booty it captures from Muslims.
They need not pay tithes on the produce of their own lands.

entries.title: Running a Templar Chapter Meeting
entries.summary: Storyguide options for staging a Templar chapter meeting (mundane, mystic or dark), with a pointer to the covenant rules for designing a priory or chapterhouse.
quotes: There are broadly three options, and elements from each can be combined.

entries.title: The Templar Grand Master
entries.summary: Powers and duties of the Templar grand master, including his spiritual authority over the order equal to that of a priest.
quotes: He may exercise Holy Influence over the order as if he were a priest.

entries.title: The Templar Rule and Penances
entries.summary: Outline of the Templar Rule and its penalties, from losing the mantle for a year and a day to expulsion, with a list of the offenses that earn them.
quotes: There are seven major sections to the rule
Major punishments include the stripping of a Templar's mantle for a year and a day

entries.title: The Manor Court
entries.summary: The three spheres of medieval justice (Church, royal and manorial courts) and which kinds of case the manorial court handles.
quotes: The manorial courts deal with lesser matters.

entries.title: Juries
entries.summary: How manorial juries are empaneled and the three jobs they perform: swearing duties are done, deciding custom, and investigating a matter for the next session.
quotes: A jury may serve three purposes, described below.
Juries of inquisition are groups of men appointed by the court to investigate a matter and report their findings at the next session.

entries.title: Disputes
entries.summary: How disputes between serfs, or between serf and lord, reach the court, which fines they generate for the lord, and the cost of a binding ruling.
quotes: A smaller fine is paid when a dispute is settled amicably outside the court.
the villein pays about a shilling for the court's time and trouble, or two shillings if the case went against him.

entries.title: Disputes Based on Weights and Measures
entries.summary: Explains that there are no standard measures and how natural measures, which tend to favor the lord, are used to settle what is owed.
quotes: There are no standard measures in any kingdom of Mythic Europe.

entries.title: Warrens
entries.summary: The lord's right of warren over small game, covering poaching and even magical creatures that could be familiars or vis sources.
quotes: Magical monsters, including potential familiars and vis sources, may also belong to the lord under the right of warren.

entries.title: Mineral Rights
entries.summary: Who owns minerals found on or beneath land: the king reserves major rights and the lord may charge for any underground resource.
quotes: In Mythic Europe a character who finds a gold nugget, or even a gold mine, doesn't own it

entries.title: Heriot, Mortuary, and Laity Objects
entries.summary: The death duties owed by a peasant to the lord (heriot) and Church (mortuary, laity objects), and their effect on widows.
quotes: The heriot is a death duty owed when the head of a household dies.
Mortuary is technically a fine, not a tax

entries.title: Tallage
entries.summary: The lord's right to demand an arbitrary sum from villeins in proportion to their holdings, its limits in practice, and its commutation to a fixed fee.
quotes: Lords have a right called tallage, which they exercise sparingly, but may legally employ whenever they wish.

entries.title: Seizure
entries.summary: A felon's goods pass to his lord, and a new tenant pays a fee to take up vacated land.
quotes: The goods of a felon automatically become the possession of his lord.

entries.title: Sex Taxes: Merchet, Leywrite, Childwrite, and Fines for Celibacy
entries.summary: The fines a lord levies on serfs over marriage, unmarried sex and pregnancy, and celibacy, and who inherits the property of serfs who die childless.
quotes: To secure the permission of the lord, each serf pays a fine called merchet.
Leywrite, the right for laying down, is theoretically an adultery tax.

entries.title: Fines for Being Fined
entries.summary: A peasant fined outside the manorial court owes his lord equivalent compensation, because what he pays is held to belong to the lord.
quotes: The lord owns everything that the peasant owns.

entries.title: Mecca and Medina Auras
entries.summary: Dominion auras in Mecca and Medina are stronger than normal, with specific scores for the haram and the Mosque of the Prophet.
quotes: Here the Dominion aura has a score of 10
This holy site has a Dominion aura of 9.

entries.title: Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock Auras
entries.summary: Gives the mixed Dominion auras on Jerusalem's Temple Mount and notes Muslims may pray at the Dome of the Rock for a blessing of Muhammad.
quotes: The Dome of the Rock has a Dominion aura of 10

entries.title: Templar Equipment
entries.summary: Lists the standard issue arms, armor, clothing, horses and squires for Templar brother-knights and brother-sergeants, and how squires differ from chivalric squires.
quotes: Each brother-knight is issued with three horses and a squire

entries.title: Templar Ciphers
entries.summary: Rules for sending Templar encrypted messages and for breaking the cipher, either without the key by an outsider or by a Templar with high Organization Lore.
quotes: the player must succeed in an Intelligence + Artes Liberales (Arithmetic) roll against an Ease Factor of 21.
with an Intelligence + Organization Lore: Knights Templar roll against an Ease Factor of 12.

entries.title: Historical Settings
entries.summary: Optional guidance for running a saga set in an earlier era when these traditions still have living practitioners, with the troupe filling in missing hedge-magic details.
quotes: You will need to fill in a few rule details

entries.title: Locating the Basilica of Ten Thousand Columns
entries.summary: A shortcut season of research to learn where the basilica lies, resolved by an Order of Hermes Lore stress roll; failure wastes the season and a botch gives a false location.
quotes: Locating the Basilica: Intelligence + Order of Hermes Lore + stress die vs. Ease Factor 21

entries.title: Interdiction
entries.summary: Interdict punishes a whole region and weakens the Dominion there over time while the sacraments are withheld.
quotes: An interdiction reduces the level of the Dominion throughout the realm by 1 each year until it is lifted.

entries.title: Naming Conventions
entries.summary: Summarizes how names are given and used among Christians, Muslims and Jews, as background for deciding which names can serve as sympathetic connections in defixio and Unlimited Range magic.

entries.title: Market Rules (Devil's Lane guild)
entries.summary: The list of guild rules governing trade, residence, debts and enforcement within the faerie toy market.
quotes: All debts must be paid within a year and a day.

entries.title: Aqueduct (repair and maintenance)
entries.summary: Rules for the labor needed to repair the temple's aqueduct and for the ongoing seasonal maintenance, with a die roll that determines whether neglect clogs it.
quotes: It requires 20 man years to repair the aqueduct
Maintenance occupies 5 characters every season, and the work must be done every season.
roll a simple die against an Ease Factor of 3 + 1 for each consecutive season for which maintenance has been neglected

entries.title: Sabbat Times
entries.summary: A table of the traditional dates on which covens hold sabbats, grouped under the winter and summer solstices.

entries.title: Finding the Grigori: search Ease Factors
entries.summary: Suggested Abilities and Ease Factors for quickly resolving the search for the Grigori relics and sites with simple Ability rolls instead of a full adventure.
quotes: Order of Hermes Lore, Ease Factor 12
Dominion Lore, Ease Factor 21

entries.title: Canarian dialects and silbo (whistled speech)
entries.summary: How well speakers of one Canarian dialect understand another, how silbo (whistled speech) is learned, and how magi can use silbo to extend the range of Voice-range spells.
quotes: A person skilled in any Canarian dialect can communicate with speakers of other Canarian dialects as if his Ability were two points lower.
Spells in silbo are considered to be cast in booming voice.

related.text: Ancient Magic Chapter 1: The Language of Adam (casting in other languages)

entries.title: Bath: A Fourth Set of Baths (Gift-suppressing baths and vis)
entries.summary: An optional hidden set of baths that suppresses the social penalties of The Gift for a time, allows a spent Confidence point to be regained once per story, and can yield Vim vis from the skin of Gifted bathers tied to their Warping Score.
quotes: The waters here suppress the negative communication effects of The Gift, for a week with each bathing.
The oil can only be drawn from a magus once after each time his Warping Score increases, and forms an Arcane Connection to the magus.

entries.title: Jewish Proscriptions Against Magic
entries.summary: Lists the mitzvot that forbid Jews from many kinds of magic and notes how this conflicts with being a Gifted Hermetic magus, with Karaite practice offering an accommodation.
quotes: It is difficult for a Gifted Jew to remain true to both his faith and his magical arts.

entries.title: Rhaetian
entries.summary: Language note: how well a Rhaetian speaker and a Latin speaker understand each other, based on Rhaetian score.
quotes: A character with a score of 5 in Rhaetian can speak to a person who knows Latin as if he had a score of 2 in that language

entries.title: The Curse of Leprosy
entries.summary: Explains leprosy as a Divine Curse in Mythic Europe and the legal and social restrictions the Office of the Seclusion places on lepers.
quotes: It cannot be cured, and is only contracted by those who are spiritually impure.

related.text: City & Guild, Chapter 1: Towns & Cities, Disease

entries.title: Church
entries.summary: The role of the local priest on a manor: curates versus rectors, their duties, who pays them, and the common limits of their education.
quotes: Each is required to preach four sermons a year, although this rule is only weakly enforced.

entries.title: The Lord's Portion: The Demesne
entries.summary: What the demesne is, how it is worked by villeins, famuli and paid labor, and why free tenants' land is more productive than the lord's.
quotes: Villeins do about a quarter of the work required to plow, sow, and reap the demesne.

entries.title: Monastic Roles and Positions
entries.requires: Playing a monk or nun with an office in a religious house
entries.summary: Describes the offices of a religious house (abbot or abbess, prior, terrar, cellarer, bursar, infirmarian, sacrist, hostillar, chancellor and others) with the Abilities, Social Status Virtue and reputation suited to each, useful for building monastic characters and contacts.
quotes: She has a reputation of level 4, either good or bad, in both the local community and the Church.

entries.title: How Powerful is a King?
entries.summary: Scale figures for a strong king (demesne share, income, household knights, greater baron vassals and their service) using the King of England as the example.
quotes: A king is technically a Great Noble and need not be a Knight, although virtually all are.

entries.title: A Destination for Pilgrimage
entries.summary: Describes how a pilgrimage to the Purgatory works, including Oppositional Elements, the Circuit of Saint Patrick and the procedures and dates that govern admission.
quotes: Those wishing to visit the Purgatory must plan to arrive at the island between June 1 and August 15; they will not be admitted outside these dates.

related.text: The Church pp.16-19 Pilgrimages and Oppositional Elements

entries.title: Research on the Purple Islands
entries.summary: Rolls and Ease Factors for what characters can learn about the Purple Islands from classical geography and Magic Lore before they sail.
quotes: An Intelligence + Artes Liberales roll, against an Ease Factor of 6, gives the following information:
An Intelligence + Magic Lore roll, against an Ease Factor of 9, gives the following information:

entries.title: The Anchoress' Rule (Ancrene Riwle)
entries.requires: Playing an anchoress or her servant
entries.summary: The rule governing an anchoress and her servants, covering speech, food, fasting, visitors, possessions and dress, which a player can adopt in part to make a character distinctively religious. Ends with ways a magical anchoress might slip out of her cell.
quotes: The primary requirements of obedience, chastity, and permanence of abode remain.

entries.title: Staging a Tournament
entries.summary: How often tournaments of different sizes occur and when in the year they are held.
quotes: a large tournament — in excess of a thousand knights — can be found on average once per season

entries.title: Tests of the Truffle Matron
entries.summary: The Matron's trials before she makes requests: a scuffling duel, a tug-of-war resolved by opposed Simple Die rolls with Size bonuses, a plant-healing challenge, and a tribute procession, which together set the size of the vis reward.
quotes: For every Size point the awakened tree is larger than the character, add +2 to the tree's die roll.
If the difference is less than 5, the two roll again and continue to roll until the accumulated difference between their rolls is 5 or more.

entries.title: The Viaticarus
entries.summary: Explains the legal, social and theological position of a person who survived Extreme Unction: denied the sacraments, unable to do penance, and legally treated as dead.
